author: Wren-EDU-c2 (independent education critic, Claude Opus 5.5 subagent)

findings.claim: E1/E5 (policy 1.3): the range check gives a false diagnosis for the most common boundary slip. Run in headless Chromium at 570 px on a first checked try: setTarget with `if (target <= 10 || target > 30) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("range"); } this.target = target;` gets 'Almost: 4 of 5 checks pass. Values below 10 still get through.' The same message appears as a failure verdict on a second try. The learner's code does refuse every value below 10; its real defect is that it also refuses 10, which the task says must be stored. A beginner is told to fix a problem that is not there and is not pointed at the comparison that is wrong. The check only recognises the exact shapes `p < 10`, `10 > p` and `p <= 9`, so any other low-side comparison falls through to this message.
findings.recommendation: Recognise the off-by-one forms that refuse an allowed boundary (`target <= 10`, `target >= 30`, `10 >= target`, `30 <= target`) and name the actual detail at the comparison to edit, for example 'Almost: your test also refuses 10, but 10 is allowed. Change the comparison with 10 in your if.' Fall back to a neutral message that names the if line rather than asserting that values below 10 get through.

findings.claim: E3 (policy 1.1): a correct guard in a different valid style is rejected and given a nudge that does not apply. On the first checked try, `if (!(target >= 10 && target <= 30)) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("range"); }` followed by `this.target = target;` gets 'Almost: 4 of 5 checks pass. Compare the parameter target with 10 and with 30 in the if that throws; 10 and 30 themselves are allowed.' The learner already compares with 10 and 30 and the code is correct, so the try is spent and the message cannot help. Related: when the second checked try is a near-miss (the `target <= 10 || target > 30` case), the verdict leads with 'Not this time', a failure verdict, rather than the near-miss verdict that policy 1.1 asks for.
findings.recommendation: Accept a negated in-range test (`!(... && ...)`) as passing, or at minimum say plainly that this editor only reads the two-comparison form shown in the Player example, and that the learner's version is valid Java. Keep the 'Almost' near-miss verdict for a right-in-substance second try. Leave the attempt rule itself unchanged, because E2 and E4 are pending.

findings.claim: E1/F5: code that javac would reject is reported as correct. With the semicolon missing after `throw new IllegalArgumentException("range")`, Problems shows 'No problems found in the parts this editor reads', Output shows all five checks passing, and the feedback says 'All 5 checks pass. No caller can now store a target outside 10 to 30'. The activity completes. The scope line does say the editor does not compile Java. Even so, a beginner who copies this into an IDE gets a compile error the page told them was not there. (Simulator fidelity is for the SME critic to confirm; this finding is about the misleading learner message.)
findings.recommendation: Have the practice editor report a missing statement terminator as a problem on the line to change, before running the checks, or soften the pass message so it does not claim the code works ('All 5 checks pass in the parts this editor reads; your IDE's compiler is the final word').

findings.claim: GIFT retention (workflow §2.3, html-artifact-contract artifact.gift): both o3 items reuse the scenarios and reasoning of the page's own Activity 2 lanes. 'An Account gets its accountNumber when it is created' is the lane scenario 'A BankAccount stores the id that identifies it'. 'balance should change only through deposit and withdraw' mirrors the BankAccount balance scenario, including its deposit/withdraw explanation. A learner can answer them by recognising the page's sorting rather than retrieving the decision rule in a new context.
findings.recommendation: Recast the o3 items with fields the page never sorted (for example a Ticket's priority that may only be raised by escalate(), or a User's signupDate). The learner then has to apply the 'fixed / rule-driven / free choice' rule rather than recall a scenario.

findings.claim: B5/G1: the recap names activities differently from the lesson path. After a full run, the recap reads 'Setter decisions: answered, not yet correct. Guard a field: answered, not yet correct. Final check: correct on the second try.' The path rows the learner navigated were 'Decide which fields get a setter', 'Guard a thermostat's target' and 'Spot the field with no setter'. A beginner told to 'open one and use Restart activity' has to work out which row each recap name means.
findings.recommendation: Make each PEP_PAGE label match its lesson-path row title, or a clearly shortened form of it.

findings.claim: Companion reading order: in artifact.md, the Teaching section opens with 'guess what this program prints' but gives no options, and it uses getters and setters before the Model section that defines them. The '## Cheat sheet' heading holds both hints ('Where to act / Next step'), the hotel anecdote, the Challenge text and a stray UI label ('Another hint Another hint, 2 of 2 for Activity 3'). The On the job card's decision and career rows (A1) are absent. The Activity 4 static alternative names loanNumber and renewals, but the question that lists those fields is missing. A learner who reads only the Markdown meets terms before they are defined, and the hints are presented as a cheat sheet. This looks generator-level (authoring/tools/qa/md-from-html.mjs), so it probably affects every page.
findings.recommendation: Have the generator keep page order (each activity's teaching, then its On the job card, its task and question stem, then its static alternative). Put hints, anecdotes and the Challenge under their own labelled headings, and drop the summary ordinal labels. Fix this in a tooling branch.

findings.claim: A5: the learner has already met this exact class. The prerequisite access-modifiers page uses a `Thermostat` whose private `setTarget` keeps the target between 10 and 30 by clamping it (`Math.max(10, Math.min(30, t))`). Activity 3 here asks for a Thermostat setter that refuses the same 10 to 30 range by throwing. The page never points back to that class or contrasts silently clamping with refusing, which is the setter design choice this topic teaches. Activity 1's feedback even says 'Java does not clamp' without making the connection.
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to the Activity 3 teaching that links back to the access-modifiers Thermostat. Say that clamping quietly changes the caller's value, while throwing reports the mistake, and that this page uses the second.
